Chapter 39

The offline itinerary

A service worker for the one scenario the product names — a trip read in a train tunnel: self from $app/service-worker, the build from $app/manifest, the deploy’s version from $app/env, three caching rules and the one the server can veto with no-store; why a remote query is never cached; a separate type-check for a worker; the copies a shared device must forget; a header that says “Offline”; a new worker after a deploy; and an end-to-end suite that waits for the worker instead of the clock.

By the end of this chapter

Add a service worker to a SvelteKit 3 app that makes pages readable offline without ever serving stale data online or one person’s pages to the next, type-check it, register it the way SvelteKit does, and test it without a flaky line.

The product names one scenario for this: the train from Lisbon to Porto goes through tunnels, and the person checking which platform the connection leaves from loses the network at exactly that moment. So the promise is narrow and exact — a trip opened once can be read again with no network — and everything in this chapter is either that promise or a guard on it. It is not an installable app (there is no web manifest) and it does not take changes offline; chapter 01 lists both under what the project does not build, and why.

A service worker is a script the browser runs beside the pages of one origin, in its own global scope with no document, and it can answer the pages’ requests itself: every fetch from a page it controls passes through its fetch event first. That makes it a programmable cache in front of the network, which is the whole of offline reading — and also the whole of the danger. A cache that answers a request the server should have answered serves yesterday’s data to somebody who is online, and a cache on a shared laptop serves one person’s pages to the next. Both are worse than no worker at all, so the file is mostly rules about what it will *not* answer.

The setup is a file

SvelteKit’s documentation puts it in one sentence: “if you have a src/service-worker/index.ts file it will be bundled and automatically registered.” Nothing goes in vite.config.ts. The build compiles the file with Vite into build/client/service-worker.js, at the root of the app’s scope, and every server-rendered page carries a few lines in its inline start-up script that register it once the page has loaded — the registration the documentation prints under “Manual registration”, with navigator.serviceWorker.register(…, { type: 'module' }). A module worker, because the bundle is an ES module. The script is the same inline block that starts the client, so the Content Security Policy already allows it (a nonce on dynamic pages, a hash on prerendered ones), and worker-src 'self' — there for MapLibre’s worker since chapter 04 — is what lets the browser fetch /service-worker.js as a worker at all.

The option behind this is serviceWorker in the SvelteKit config, and the project leaves it alone. register is true by default; options is the RegistrationOptions object handed to register(), and SvelteKit adds type: 'module' to whatever is there. serviceWorker: { register: false } exists for registering by hand — after a consent screen, say, or only for some people — and nothing here needs that. An earlier plan for this chapter registered the worker by hand with { type: dev ? 'module' : 'classic' }; it is wrong twice over, because the documentation’s registration is a module in every case, and because “the service worker is bundled for production, but not during development” — pnpm dev never runs it, so there is no development case to switch on.

SvelteKit 2 had a module of its own for this, $service-worker, and SvelteKit 3 removed it; importing it is a build error that names the replacements. Its five exports, and where each went:

  • base (the base path) → resolve() from $app/paths — and, inside a worker, the registration’s scope, below.
  • build (Vite’s output) → immutable from $app/manifest.
  • files (the static/ folder) → assets from $app/manifest.
  • prerendered → prerendered from $app/manifest.
  • version → version from $app/env.

Three modules may not be imported into a worker at all: $app/forms, $app/navigation and $app/state belong to a page, and the build refuses them with “Cannot import … into service-worker code”.

What the worker knows: the build, and the deploy

self from $app/service-worker is globalThis, typed as a ServiceWorkerGlobalScope — the module exists so that self.addEventListener('fetch', …) hands you a FetchEvent and not a DOM event. version from $app/env is config.version.name, which is the commit this build was made from (chapter 04), and it goes into every cache name, so each deploy gets caches of its own. $app/manifest lists the build: immutable is every file Vite wrote — the hashed JavaScript, CSS, fonts, the MapLibre worker, the globe’s chunk — assets is every file in static/, and prerendered is every page and endpoint rendered at build time. In this project that last list is the guides in three languages, /api/world.json, and one entry worth noticing: _app/remote/<hash>/places, the prerendered remote function from chapter 17, written to disk at build time like a page.

immutable and prerendered are empty in development, says the documentation, which is one more reason the worker only exists in a build. Each path is relative to the base path, and the documentation’s example turns them into absolute pathnames with resolve() from $app/paths. In TypeScript that does not compile, and the compiler is right: resolve() takes one of this app’s routes or pathnames — the same typed union href() is built on (chapter 25) — and _app/immutable/nodes/0.BaOiqs_e.js is neither. assets is typed more narrowly still: { path: AssetPath }, where AssetPath is generated from static/ and here is exactly "embed/meridian-route.js" | "robots.txt", so asset('robots.txt') type-checks and asset('robot.txt') does not. The worker sidesteps both with a fact about where it lives: SvelteKit serves it from the root of the app, so its registration’s scope *is* the base path, and resolving a path against the scope gives the pathname a request will have. (%sveltekit.assets%, the placeholder app.html can use for a favicon, is the same idea in the template — “either paths.assets, if specified, or a relative path to paths.base” — and a separate paths.assets host is the one configuration SvelteKit refuses outright with a worker: “Cannot use service worker alongside config.paths.assets”.)

install copies the build into this deploy’s cache, and waitUntil holds the worker in the installing state until the copy is done — if one file fails, addAll fails, and the worker is discarded rather than activated with half a build. activate runs when the worker takes over and deletes every cache that is not its own, which is how a deploy’s files leave the device. The copy is the whole build, about 8 MB on disk at the time of writing, and most of it is the globe: three.js, and two 3D-model decoders, Draco and Basis, that arrive in the build with the 3D libraries although this globe loads no model. The documentation’s caution applies — “you should also be careful about caching large assets” — and the trade made here is that every tab works in the tunnel, the globe included. If the size ever matters, the decoders are the first thing to leave out of FILES.

Three rules, and the requests it never answers

The fetch handler sorts every request into one of four kinds. A hashed file of the build — immutable, Vite’s output — is answered from the copy, always: cache first, because its name contains a hash of its content, so a newer version would have a different name and there is never a reason to ask the network again. The rest of the build — static/ and every prerendered page and endpoint — has no hash in its name: guides/lisbon-in-three-days and api/world.json are called the same after the next deploy. Those are network first, with the install-time copy as the offline answer; served from the copy, a guide edited in the next deploy would stay old *online* for as long as the old worker held the tab. A page — a navigation, request.mode === 'navigate' — is asked of the network first and kept (below). And everything else gets no respondWith at all, which means the browser fetches it exactly as if there were no worker: network only. That last rule is the one that keeps the app honest online.

Why a remote query is never answered from a cache

Every read in this app is a remote function, and its request is a GET to /_app/remote/… with the arguments in the URL — exactly the kind of request a naive worker caches. Then tripBySlug would answer from the copy *online*: a stop a companion added an hour ago missing, a deleted trip still there, with nothing on screen to say so. The live stream is worse: watchTrip is one long response that never ends, and a cache can only store a response that has. So remote calls and __data.json — which carries a layout’s per-person data — go straight to the network and fail without one, and the page handles the failure as it always has. The exception proves the rule: places() is a prerender function, its answer is fixed at build time, it is listed in prerendered, and so it is a file of the build and comes from the copy, which keeps the place search working in the tunnel.

A page is network first: online, the person always gets today’s page and the worker keeps a copy; offline, the fetch throws and the copy is served, or the error is thrown on if there is none. The copy is written with event.waitUntil, beside the response rather than in front of it, so the page streams to the screen while it is being kept. What is kept is decided by worthKeeping, and each condition is a lesson. A redirect never arrives as a 200 — a navigation’s redirects come to the worker as an opaque response with status 0 — so the sign-in page is never stored under the address of the trip that redirected to it. An error page is not the page. An endpoint answers JSON, not text/html, and the /api/ test before it keeps Better Auth’s routes out entirely. And Cache-Control: no-store is the server saying “never write this down”: the health endpoint sends it (chapter 38), and any page that ever should not be kept can say so without a change here. ignoreVary is explained in the comment: Vary: Cookie (chapter 47) protects caches shared between people, and this one is not.

The obvious way to tell a page from an endpoint is to match the URL against the app’s routes — $app/manifest exports routes, each a ManifestRoute with an id and page and endpoint flags, and $app/paths exports match(). It cannot be done in a worker: match() there throws “Cannot use match(...) inside a service worker, as it depends on the SvelteKit client instance”. The response’s own content type is the better test anyway — it is what the server actually sent.

A worker has its own types

A worker’s global scope has caches, clients and FetchEvent, and no window or document, so it cannot be type-checked against the DOM library the rest of the app uses. SvelteKit generates a second base config for it, $app/tsconfig/service-worker, with "lib": ["ESNext", "WebWorker"], and the documentation’s two steps are the two files: the root tsconfig.json excludes src/service-worker (chapter 04), and this one extends the worker’s base with the same strictness as the rest of the project. The catch is that svelte-check only reads one tsconfig per run, so excluding the folder from the root config quietly stops anything from checking it at all. check therefore runs a second program: tsc -p src/service-worker. Not a second svelte-check --tsconfig: given a folder with no .svelte file in it, svelte-check warns that it found nothing to check, and here a warning fails the build (chapter 03). Plain TypeScript is tsc’s job, and tsc follows the worker’s imports, so #lib/offline/pages.ts is checked as worker code too. Both directions of the check have teeth:

The shared device

The pages the worker keeps were rendered on the server *for the person signed in*: a private trip’s itinerary, their companions, their name in the header. On a phone that is fine. On the family laptop, the hotel’s lobby computer, a colleague’s machine borrowed for a minute, it means the next person can switch off the Wi-Fi, type the address of a trip they were never invited to, and read it. Vary: Cookie cannot help — it is a header for caches between people, and this cache is inside the one browser profile they share. So the app itself empties the cache, and the cache’s name lives in a module both sides import: the worker opens the cache by it, the app deletes by it. It deletes by the *prefix*, not the full name, and the comment says why: after a deploy, a tab running the new code can sit beside a worker that is still the old one, holding a cache with the old version in its name.

The event that matters is signing out, and the header’s form handles it with the remote form’s own hook. signOut.enhance(callback) replaces the default submission with yours; the callback receives a copy of the form, and form.submit() performs the submission without calling the callback again. So the copies are deleted, and only then is the session ended — in that order, so that there is no moment at which a person is signed out and their pages are still on the device. Without JavaScript the form still signs out, and there is nothing to delete: registering a worker is itself a script, so a device that never ran the app’s JavaScript holds no copies. The case in between — a sign-out pressed before the page has hydrated — is the layout’s, next.

A session can also end without the button: it expires, it is revoked from another device, or the person presses “Sign out” on a slow phone before the page has hydrated and the form submits the plain way, with no callback. Every one of those ends the same way — the next page renders with nobody signed in — so the (site) layout, which knows who is signed in, deletes the copies whenever it finds nobody. It is an effect because it is a write to something outside the component in answer to a value, and it runs again when data.user changes. Its cost is a caches.keys() on a signed-out page load, and its trade is deliberate: a stranger reading a public trip gets no offline copy, because the policy is simple to state and to test — *the device keeps pages only while somebody is signed in*. What it cannot cover is a session that expires and is then opened offline before any page has been loaded online; the copies stay until the next deploy, or the next page load with a network. The sign-out button is the guarantee; the layout is the net.

A header that says “Offline”

A page served from the copy hydrates from the copied build and runs like any other — and its live stream cannot connect. Before this chapter the chip would have said “Connecting…” for three seconds and then offered the coral “Reconnect”, a button that cannot work in a tunnel. Now the status has a fourth state, first in the derivation: online from svelte/reactivity/window is navigator.onLine as a reactive value, and when it is false the chip says “Offline” in the quiet grey and offers nothing. It is undefined on the server, which is why the test is === false: a page rendered on a server must not claim to be offline. The sizer gained a fourth label, so the slot stays the width of the widest in every language.

Coming back online is the subtle half. SvelteKit’s documentation promises that when a live query’s connection drops it “will attempt to reconnect passively, with exponential backoff, and actively if navigator.onLine goes from false to true” — and the client’s source has the condition the sentence leaves out: that applies to a stream that had connected. A live query whose *first* connection fails has never delivered a value, and it fails for good: done becomes true, and only reconnect() starts it again. A page opened in a tunnel is exactly that case. So ononline, a handler on <svelte:window>, asks: if the stream is not connected when the network returns, reconnect() it. reconnect() stops whatever attempt is under way before it starts one, so the handler does not need to know whether the first attempt had finished failing — which is what keeps the end-to-end test free of a race. It is an event, so it is a handler, not an effect watching online.current: nothing is being derived.

A new worker after a deploy

The documentation is precise about when a browser looks for a new worker: “when a full-page navigation happens within its scope, and after functional events such as push and sync. Client-side navigations are neither.” A trip planner is a page people leave open for days, so a deploy could go unnoticed by its worker for as long as the tab lives. The root layout asks on every navigation — navigator.serviceWorker.getRegistration(), then registration.update() — which is the documentation’s own pattern, with three changes: no request when there is no network, because afterNavigate also runs when a page hydrates and a page read offline hydrates too; none for a shallow goto — isShallowGoto, the test chapter 27 explains — because opening the stop dialog is not a visit to a page and would fetch service-worker.js every time; and a failed check is fire-and-forget, a background chore the next navigation repeats. SvelteKit keeps the same rule for its own chore of this kind: when a client-side navigation fails and a check finds a newer build live, it asks the registered worker to update and then loads the page the plain way, and since 3.1 a failed update there no longer stops that load. A new worker found this way installs in the background and “take[s] over as soon as the number of tabs managed by the existing service worker drops to zero”. It does not swap itself in under an open page. That is why only hashed files are served from the copy: everything whose name outlives its content — pages, prerendered guides, static/ — is asked of the network first, so a waiting worker never serves an old one online, and the deploy banner (chapter 25) already turns the next navigation into a full reload.

Two refinements are named and left out. self.skipWaiting() would let a new worker take over open tabs at once, and the pattern that makes it safe is to call it from the deploy banner’s button and reload when navigator.serviceWorker fires controllerchange — a listener on an object outside any component, which is the honest use of on() from svelte/events. Nothing needs it today, for the reason above. And @vite-pwa/sveltekit, the generator most SvelteKit projects reach for, was declined in chapter 40: its SvelteKit integration reads a svelte.config.js that SvelteKit 3 does not have, and a worker of a few dozen lines written against $app/manifest, each rule with its reason beside it, is easier to read than a generated one.

Proving it without a clock

Service workers are a classic source of flaky tests, because so much of their life happens in the background, and the header of the file says how this suite avoids every one of them: it waits for the thing each step needs, and never for a number of milliseconds. The worker registers on load, so the test waits for navigator.serviceWorker.ready, which resolves when a worker is active — the build copied. A worker controls only the pages that load *after* it is active, so the page is reloaded once and the test asserts there is now a controller. The copy of the page is written beside the response, so expect.poll asks Cache Storage until it is there. Offline is context.setOffline(true), and in Playwright 1.64 that reaches the worker’s own network as well as the page’s — so with no network the worker’s fetch really fails, and what the page shows really came from the copy. response.fromServiceWorker() says so.

Three tests, one per promise. The first reads the trip offline — the heading, two seeded stops, “Offline” and no Reconnect — and then goes back online and waits for “Live”, which is the reconnect above working. The second signs out through the header and checks two things: the copy is gone the moment the sign-out has finished, and a navigation to the trip with no network now fails as it would with no worker at all. The third ends the session without the button — clearCookies() is an expired session as far as the server can tell — loads the home page, and waits for the layout to empty the cache. Each was proven against broken code before it was trusted: with the worker’s fallback removed the first fails on its offline reload, with both deletions removed the second fails on its first check, and with the layout’s effect removed the third never sees the copy go. The rest of the suite runs with workers blocked, and chapter 46 says why.

Checkpoint

  • You can say which requests the worker answers from the build, which from a kept page, and which it never answers — and why remote queries are in the last group.
  • You can map each export of the removed $service-worker module to its SvelteKit 3 replacement.
  • You know why the worker has its own tsconfig, why tsc checks it and not svelte-check, and how you would prove the check has teeth.
  • You can explain what the shared-device problem is, which two places delete the copies, and why they delete by prefix.
  • You can say why a page opened offline needs reconnect() when the network returns, when SvelteKit already reconnects a dropped stream.
  • You can name three things that make a service-worker test flaky, and what this suite waits for instead of each.
